```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

This vignette introduces and discusses the different classes in the package, how they work, what they're made of, when
you should use them, and what they can do for you ages and age groups. An age, an age range, and an assigned category
describe different things. An age tells us how old someone is at a particular time. An interval defines a range of
possible ages. A category records which range an observation belongs to. A scheme gives a reusable set of ranges with
provenance, an identity, purpose, and rules.

This guide explains the four main classes in agecraft so you can choose
objects to use in an analysis and understand what information
each preserves. 

| Class | What it represents | What it contains |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| `age` | Age values for observations | Fractional numeric values and one time unit (e.g. year, month, week, etc) |
| `age_interval` | Age range definitions, including category definitions | Lower and upper bounds, one optional time unit, optional names, and display settings |
| `age_group` | Age group or category assignments for ages | Ordered-factor codes and labels, with one age interval definition per level |
| `age_scheme` | A reusable age interval classification definition | Named intervals, identity, purpose, provenance, and validation rules |

These are S3 classes. A class tells R what an object represents and how to handle operations such as printing or
subsetting. `age` and `age_interval` use the [vctrs](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/) framework for vector behavior;
`age_interval` builds on [ivs](https://davisvaughan.github.io/ivs/) intervals. `age_group` is an ordered-factor
subclass. An `age_scheme` is a list-based metadata object containing an interval vector.

## Observations to follow through the classes

The following fictional visit records include two infants, a child
exactly five years old, an adult, and a missing birth date. Each row is
one visit. 

```{r sample-data}
visits <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  birth_date = as.Date(c("2025-06-20", "2025-01-01", "2020-07-01",
                         "1980-01-01", NA)),
  visit_date = rep(as.Date("2025-07-01"), 5)
)
visits
```

The dates remain useful even after calculating ages. They let us
calculate age directly in another date/time unit when the analysis requires it.

## The age class: values with a unit

An `age` vector has the numeric ages with fractional precision and unit attached. Each element represents an age value;
the entire vector shares one unit, such as year or day. Values in the vector are finite and non-negative; missing values
are allowed and denoted with the usual R `NA`.

```{r calculate-ages}
# add ages to the data frame
visits$age <- calculate_age(visits$birth_date, visits$visit_date, unit = "year")
visits[c("id", "age")]
is_age(visits$age)
```


### Stored values and printed ages

The default display expresses ages as completed whole units, much as people
ordinarily report their age. Both infants therefore print as zero years,
although their stored ages differ. You can display those fractions or extract
the values explicitly:

```{r inspect-ages}
# Default display: completed whole units.
visits$age

# Display fractional values without changing the age vector.
format(visits$age, fractional = TRUE)

# Extract full numeric values, including fractions.
as.numeric(visits$age)

# Extract completed whole units as integers.
as.integer(visits$age)
```

`format()` returns a character representation while leaving the original object
unchanged. `as.numeric()` returns the full stored values as an ordinary numeric
vector; `as.integer()` returns completed whole units as integers. Both extraction
methods remove the age class and its unit information.

The stored fractions allow classification within a whole unit. Two infants who
both print as zero years can still belong to different age groups. For example,
you might distinguish ages below 28 days from ages beginning at 28 days. For an
exact 28-day boundary, calculate ages and define the groups in days: a fraction
of a calendar year does not correspond to the same number of days for every
birth date.

#### Calendar anniversaries and elapsed time

When calculating an age from dates, the chosen unit determines how the
calculation works. Years and months follow calendar anniversaries, such as
birthdays or the same day in successive months. Their lengths vary: a year can
contain 365 or 366 days, and a month can contain 28 to 31 days. Weeks, days,
hours, minutes, and seconds have fixed relationships and can each be expressed
as a known number of seconds. Agecraft therefore calculates years and months
using calendar anniversaries and smaller units using elapsed time.

For years, `calculate_age()` counts completed birthdays and adds the fraction
of calendar days completed between the previous birthday and the next. For
months, it counts completed monthly anniversaries and adds the corresponding
fraction between consecutive anniversaries. These rules account for dates that
do not occur in every year or month:

- **Leap birthdays:** For someone born on February 29, the yearly anniversary
  falls on March 1 in a non-leap year and February 29 in a leap year. Someone
  born on February 29, 2020 therefore completes one year on March 1, 2021,
  rather than February 28.
- **Month ends:** If the original day does not exist in the target month,
  the monthly anniversary falls on that month's last day. For someone born
  on January 31, 2025, the first two monthly anniversaries are February 28
  and March 31. Each anniversary is calculated from the original birth date,
  so the February adjustment does not move later anniversaries to the 28th.

For `POSIXct` date-times, calendar years and months use local dates in the
starting date-time's time zone. The end is interpreted in that same time zone,
and time of day is ignored. Someone born at 15:00 therefore completes a calendar
year on their anniversary date even when the reference time that day is before
15:00.

Elapsed time measures the duration between the two points, including their
times of day. This is useful when deciding, for example, whether a newborn is
less than 48 hours old. An elapsed day is exactly 24 hours, and an elapsed week
is seven such days. Consecutive local midnights can nevertheless be 23 or 25
hours apart when clocks change for daylight saving, producing `23 / 24` or
`25 / 24` elapsed days. Choose years or months for anniversary-based ages, and
smaller units when the elapsed duration matters.

### Constructing and using age values

If ages are already available as numbers, give them their known unit:

```{r construct-age}
known_ages <- age(c(0.5, 5, 45), unit = "year")
known_ages
visits$age[1:3]
mean(visits$age, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Subsetting, sorting, and supported summaries retain the age class and
unit. Numeric addition and subtraction use that unit: `known_ages + 1`
adds one year. Negative results are rejected. Constructing an age from a
completed-year number cannot recover fractions that were discarded
earlier.

Use `as_age()` for explicit unit conversion. Days convert to weeks by a
fixed ratio. Conversions involving calendar months or years require
`allow_approx = TRUE`, including month-to-year conversion. Numerical
conversion does not recover the original dates. When exact day-based
classification matters, calculate ages in days directly from those
dates.

## The age_interval class: ranges with boundaries

An `age_interval` vector represents ranges. It can define reporting
categories or describe uncertain ages when only a range is known. Each
element contains a lower and upper bound. The vector also carries an
optional common unit, optional interval names, and settings for
displaying interval labels.

For our visit records, define three illustrative reporting bands:

```{r define-intervals}
bands <- age_interval(
  start = c(0, 1, 5), end = c(1, 5, Inf), unit = "year"
)
names(bands) <- c("Under 1", "1 to under 5", "5 and older")
bands

data.frame(
  label = names(bands),
  lower = ivs::iv_start(bands),
  upper = ivs::iv_end(bands)
)
```

These boundaries are teaching examples, rather than an official
reporting standard. An interval includes its lower bound and excludes
its upper bound: `[1, 5)` includes the first birthday and stops just
before the fifth. Its completed-age display is `1-4`. Exactly five
belongs to `[5, Inf)`. Fractional bounds are preserved; only upper
bounds may be infinite. A missing interval has both bounds missing.

### Definitions exist independently of observations

There are three intervals here regardless of how many visit records we
have. Naming a range makes its meaning readable without changing its
boundaries. Names do not change interval equality or chronological
ordering.

```{r select-intervals}
bands[1:2]
compare_age_intervals(bands[1:2], operation = "width")
```

Widths use the interval's coordinate unit, years here. A width in years
is not an exact elapsed-day duration. Selection and supported
concatenation retain names and units; coverage set operations may merge
or split intervals and therefore discard names.

An interval vector may have gaps or overlaps. Its class alone does not
promise that every age belongs to exactly one range. A unit of `NULL`
means the unit is unspecified. For this guide, both observations and
definitions explicitly use years so their coordinates are directly
comparable.

## The age_group class: assignments with their definitions

We have age observations and interval definitions. Classifying the
observations connects them:

```{r assign-groups}
visits$group <- categorize_age(visits$age, by = bands)
visits[c("id", "age", "group")]
class(visits$group)
table(visits$group, useNA = "ifany")
```

The result is an `age_group`, with classes `age_group`, `ordered`, and
`factor`. Each element is one observation's category assignment. Both
infants belong to "Under 1"; the child exactly five belongs to "5 and
older". The missing birth date produces a missing age and assignment. An
age outside every interval would also receive `NA`; that assignment
alone does not distinguish the causes.

### What an assignment retains

Like an ordered factor, an `age_group` contains integer category codes
and readable levels. It also retains one interval definition per level,
available through `group_intervals()`:

```{r inspect-groups}
levels(visits$group)
as.integer(visits$group)
group_intervals(visits$group)
```

The codes identify categories; they are not ages. The definitions have
three elements, while the assignment vector has five, one per visit.
Category levels follow interval order. The original exact ages and
scheme provenance are not stored in an `age_group`. Keep the age column
when later calculations or new boundaries may require it.

Subsetting preserves unused categories and their definitions. Remove
them explicitly when a reduced set is wanted:

```{r subset-groups}
infants <- visits$group[1:2]
levels(infants)
levels(droplevels(infants))
```

Combining assignments requires matching ordered bounds, labels, and
definition units. Matching label text alone is insufficient. Use
`vctrs::vec_rbind()` when binding data frames containing these objects;
base data-frame binding can reconstruct factors and discard their
definitions. To obtain an ordinary factor, use `generics::as.factor()`
or `generics::as.ordered()` explicitly.

If you need a matched interval for each observation instead, request
interval output:

```{r matched-intervals}
matched <- categorize_age(visits$age, by = bands, output = "interval")
matched
length(matched)
```

This is an `age_interval` vector with one element per visit, including
repeated and missing intervals. It represents the matched ranges rather
than factor codes with a shared level definition.

## The age_scheme class: a reusable definition with context

An interval vector tells us where boundaries fall. A scheme also records
what the definition is for, how it is identified, and which validation
rules apply. Use an `age_scheme` when the same definition must be reused
across reports or retained with its source and purpose.

```{r define-scheme}
visit_scheme <- age_scheme(
  intervals = bands,
  id = "example_visit_bands",
  name = "Illustrative visit reporting bands",
  type = "partition",
  domain = c(0, Inf),
  complete = TRUE,
  purpose = "Demonstrate age classes using fictional visits"
)
visit_scheme
scheme_intervals(visit_scheme)
```

This object contains the named `age_interval` vector. It also contains
its ID, name, purpose, partition/classification type, optional domain,
completeness claim, and provenance fields such as source, reference,
organization, version, and verification status. Information that is
unknown can remain unspecified. The scheme does not contain the visit
records or their assignments.

A scheme contains intervals; it does not inherit from `age_interval`.
Its intervals supply boundaries, labels, and units, while the scheme
supplies context and rules. `scheme_intervals()` retrieves the
definitions, and `summary()` reports coverage and provenance.

### Validation expresses the intended classification

A `partition` prohibits overlapping categories. With
`domain = c(0, Inf)` and `complete = TRUE`, construction also checks
that these bands cover the declared all-age domain. Completeness is a
separate property from nonoverlap. A `classification` may permit
overlapping memberships, and `complete = NA` makes no completeness
claim.

These checks establish properties of the definition. They do not
establish that its categories are appropriate for a reporting system or
independently verify an external source.

```{r use-scheme}
from_scheme <- categorize_age(visits$age, by = visit_scheme)
identical(from_scheme, visits$group)
```

Using this scheme produces the same assignments as its interval vector.
The assignments retain category definitions, while the scheme's identity
and provenance remain with the separate scheme object. Save the scheme
alongside the analysis when that context matters. Ordinary substantive
edits to a scheme are validated and track derivative ancestry; see the
schemes guide for details.

By default, `categorize_age()` rejects multiple matches. If a scheme
intentionally overlaps, `classify_age_scheme()` provides a table of all
memberships. Such a table is an ordinary data frame; overlapping
memberships cannot be summed as mutually exclusive population groups.

## Choosing what to retain

In the visit example, the dates allow recalculation, the `age` column
preserves precise values with units, and the `age_group` column supports
category tables while keeping the category bounds retrievable. The
separate `age_scheme` records the reusable definition and its context.

| Your next task | Object to retain |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| Calculate or compare individual ages | Original dates and an `age` vector |
| Inspect or compare age ranges | An `age_interval` vector |
| Tabulate assigned categories and retrieve their bounds | An `age_group` vector |
| Reuse or document a classification definition | An `age_scheme` object |

Other familiar R classes appear at the boundaries: `Date` and `POSIXct`
supply dates and times; `units` vectors carry time quantities; ordinary
factors carry labels; and data frames hold observations or membership
tables. A scheme summary uses the supporting `summary_age_scheme` class
for readable printing. These support the four roles above without
replacing them.

For detailed assignment operations, see [Age groups: assignments with
interval definitions](age-groups.html). For overlapping classifications,
provenance, and editing definitions, see [Reusable age
schemes](age-schemes.html). For individual arithmetic tasks, see [Age
arithmetic and classification examples](age_math_examples.html). The
help topics `?age`, `?age_interval`, `?age_group`, and `?age_scheme`
provide their full construction and behavior contracts.
